neighbours.label: 'if' (or 'where') opening an embedded clause after a verb of checking or finding out ('see if', 'check if'); quiet on 'if' in ordinary conditionals.
fire: The mechanic opened the hood to see if the belt was worn.
She called the shop to check if the parcel had arrived.
We knocked on the door to see if anyone was home.
The teacher asked the class to find out if the plant needed more light.
He tasted the soup to see if it needed more salt.
The guard walked around the building to check if the windows were locked.
I looked in the fridge to see if there was any milk left.
They phoned the hotel to find out if a room was free.
quiet: You can borrow my bike if you bring it back by six.
We will cancel the picnic if it rains in the morning.
The plant grows faster if it gets plenty of light.
He tasted the soup and added a pinch of salt.
The guard locked the windows before leaving the building.
Take an umbrella in case the weather turns.
They phoned the hotel and booked a room for two nights.
The cake will burn if you leave it in too long.

notes: The card suggested a predictor of existential 'there', but 'see if the pipes' fired as strongly as 'see if there', so the claim is the embedded-question 'if'. Conditionals mid-sentence are untested.
